Study_Title: An Application-Layer Multi-Modal Covert-Channel Reference Monitor for LLM Agent Egress
Threat_Attacker_Model: Compromised or prompt-injected LLM agent exfiltrating secrets across allowed destinations via 15 multi-modal covert channels: text (zero-width chars, homoglyphs, whitespace, base64, JSON key ordering, timing, packet size), image (LSB planes, per-image mean luminance, inter-image sequence permutation), and audio (ultrasonic >20 kHz, audible-band FSK sonification, Table 1, p. 4).
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Boot-time cryptographic legitimacy attestation using pinned Ed25519 public keys over canonical `{kind, data-class}` media claims, SHA-256 content-addressed canonicalization (closing inter-image permutation modulo SHA-256 second-preimage, p. 8), and a 10-stage text canonicalizer + FFT audio / RGB image scramblers.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Application-Layer Multi-Modal Covert-Channel Reference Monitor interposing on all outbound agent egress messages, tool calls, and media payloads (Section 2–4, pp. 4–11).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Proposition 1 (Allowlist-by-signature, p. 11): unsigned binary media is scrambled by default; residual Miller–Madow mutual-information capacity is driven to exactly 0.0 bits/symbol on all 14 destroyable channels and bounded to a stated ceiling on per-image mean luminance.
Trust_Assumptions: Auditor publishes trusted Ed25519 public keys and `{kind, data-class}` pairs at boot into an immutable trust root; reference monitor mediates all outbound agent egress channels.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Evaluated against an adversarial ensemble of 15 working covert encoders across text, image, and audio (T=20 trials/cell, Tables 3–6, pp. 13–16): drives Miller–Madow corrected mutual information I(X;Y) to 0.0 bits (100% capacity destruction) on all destroyable text, imageLSB/permutation, and audio channels, and bounds the non-destroyable per-image mean-luminance channel via coarse bucketing.
Exposed_Security_Function: 10-stage lossless/lossy text canonicalizer, per-sink leaky-bucket capacity ledger, Ed25519 boot-time media legitimacy verifier, and FFT-audio / RGB-image scramblers.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Per-image mean luminance cannot be reduced to zero capacity without destroying image visibility, so it is bounded via bucketing and leaky-bucket rate accounting rather than eliminated (explicitly stated p. 1 & p. 8); relies on pre-quantum Ed25519 signatures (STAGE_0).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1) & Section 4 Proposition 1 (p. 11): "Two media scramblers (a Fourier-domain audio band-limiter and a red-green-blue (RGB) image bit-depth and mean-luminance bucketer) gated by a boot-time cryptographic legitimacy attestation: an auditor publishes at boot the trusted Ed25519 keys and {kind, data-class} pairs; only payloads with a verifying signature for an authorized class are exempt... The reference implementation drives residual capacity to zero on every destroyable channel and to a stated bound on the one (per-image mean luminance) that cannot be destroyed without ruining the image."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Combines a 10-stage text canonicalizer, per-sink leaky-bucket capacity ledger, FFT/RGB media scramblers, and Ed25519 legitimacy attestation (Proposition 1) to reduce residual covert-channel mutual information to zero across 14/15 multi-modal channels and bound mean-luminance capacity.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Formal allowlist-by-signature proof (Proposition 1) and 15-encoder multi-modal mutual-information benchmark (T=20 trials/cell, 26 pp.).
Protected_Object: Outbound agent text, JSON, image, audio, and timing egress channels.
Composition_Evidence: Gates outbound media egress on Ed25519 producer attestations (B3) while tracking cumulative residual bit capacity per sink in a leaky-bucket audit ledger (B4).
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (26 hlm.). Memvalidasi monitor referensi kanal terselubung multi-modal (10 tahap teks + scrambler audio/citra + atestasi Ed25519 + kanonikalisasi SHA-256), Proposition 1 (hlm. 11), dan evaluasi 15 encoder (Tables 3–6 hlm. 13–16).

Study_Title: Identity-Bound Governance Under Execution Uncertainty: An Accountability Proof Block for LLM Agent Persistent Halts, with Cryptographic Implementation and Cross-Model Calibration
Threat_Attacker_Model: Execution uncertainty and persistent governance halts where an LLM agent's observability or drift-detection layer fails and an adversary attempts to forge resumption authority, tamper with halt evidence E_s, replay stale human decisions D_h, or capture governance with fewer than k compromised principals.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Accountability Proof Block (`APB(k)`): real `cryptography/ed25519` k-of-n multi-principal digital signatures (`sigma_h = Sign_sk(E_s || D_h)`) binding system-constructed evidence block E_s and human decision block D_h to registered principals H_i in P, with UUID4 semantic-uniqueness checks (predicates V1–V5) and an HMAC-chained append-only persistence log.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Authority Resolution Function G and 5-predicate APB Verifier (V1–V5) governing persistent agent halts and resumption/recalibration transitions (Sections 3–4, pp. 3–10).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Four formal theorems (Section 4, pp. 7–10): Theorem 4.1 (Protocol-Bounded Governance Completeness), Theorem 4.2 (Evidence-Decision Non-Severability under Ed25519 EUF-CMA), Theorem 4.3 (Replay & Tamper Resistance), and Proposition 4.12 (k-of-n Byzantine Principal Resistance).
Trust_Assumptions: At least n - k + 1 registered human principals keep their Ed25519 secret keys uncompromised; Ed25519 satisfies EUF-CMA; HMAC key for local append-only persistence is intact.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Validated via Python `cryptography/ed25519` implementation (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20157139, Tables 2–7, pp. 11–16): achieves 100.0% governance completeness across all halt seeds (Table 3, p. 13), 100.0000% tamper/forgery detection with 0% false positives across 200 freshly-signed APBs under 4 attack vectors (Table 5, p. 14), and cross-model drift-threshold calibration across 6 LLM families (500 drift steps, sigma/T* < 2% within-model, Table 6 p. 15).
Exposed_Security_Function: Accountability Proof Block (APB) k-of-n Ed25519 signer/verifier (V1–V5), Authority Resolution Function G, HMAC-chained halt log, and 6-LLM drift threshold calibrator.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Cross-model calibration shows optimal drift threshold T* varies by ~1.8x across the 6 LLM families (requiring per-model calibration rather than a single universal constant, Table 6 p. 15); relies on classical Ed25519 signatures (STAGE_0_PRE_QUANTUM_ONLY).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1–2) & Section 5 Tables 3–6 (pp. 13–15): "We introduce the Accountability Proof Block (APB), a two-part record consisting of a system-constructed evidence block E_s, a human-supplied decision block D_h, and a cryptographic signature sigma_h binding the two to a registered principal H_i in P... We provide a real-cryptography implementation in cryptography/ed25519... All tampering vectors against 200 freshly-signed APBs achieve 100.0000% detection."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Introduces the Ed25519-signed Accountability Proof Block (APB) and k-of-n Authority Resolution Function G with 4 formal theorems, achieving 100% governance completeness and 100% tamper detection across 200 signed APBs and 4 attack vectors.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Formal theorems (Theorems 4.1–4.3, Proposition 4.12), `cryptography/ed25519` implementation (Zenodo DOI), 200-APB tamper benchmark, and 6-LLM calibration (24 pp.).
Protected_Object: Persistent halt evidence blocks (E_s), human governance decision blocks (D_h), k-of-n Ed25519 signatures (sigma_h), and HMAC-chained governance logs.
Composition_Evidence: Cryptographically binds human principal resumption authority (B1/B2) to system-observed halt evidence and HMAC-chained audit records (B4).

Memvalidasi konstruksi Accountability Proof Block (APB) berbasis Ed25519 + HMAC chain, 4 teorema formal (hlm. 7–10), deteksi tampering 100% pada 200 APB (Table 5 hlm. 14), dan kalibrasi lintas 6 keluarga LLM (Table 6 hlm. 15).

Study_Title: Agent Flight Recorder: Tamper-Evident Audit Trails with On-Chain Anchoring for Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
Threat_Attacker_Model: Post-incident log tampering (event edit, deletion, reordering, or history forking) and cross-organizational attribution disputes after long-horizon agent failures (e.g., production DB deletion or cross-agent prompt injection propagation).
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Canonical event serialization over 8 semantic fields (intent, caller, delegation, guardrail, tool, arguments, result, provenance), SHA-256 hash chaining, Merkle tree epoch batching (100-event epochs), and on-chain L2 Ethereum (Base Sepolia) anchoring storing a 32-byte epoch root and back-pointer.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Agent Flight Recorder gateway wrapper and Base Sepolia L2 anchoring smart contract (Section II–IV, pp. 2–6).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: 100% tamper detection (with 0% false positives) against event edit, deletion, reordering, and history forking for all epochs anchored prior to host compromise, plus third-party Merkle inclusion verification without exposing raw event payloads on-chain.
Trust_Assumptions: Following Schneier & Kelsey forward-integrity model (Section II, p. 2): instrumented gateway records events before host compromise, and anchored 32-byte epoch roots on Base Sepolia L2 remain immutable/available.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Evaluated across 5 cumulative ablation configurations on synthetic workloads and real SWE-agent traces from SWE-bench plus 100 Base Sepolia L2 transactions (Abstract p. 1, Table I p. 6): full system adds ~48 us median per-event latency and 512 bytes per event; L2 anchoring costs $2.30 per 100,000 events (at 100-event epochs); detects 100% of edit/delete/reorder/fork tampering with 0% FPR; structured forensic queries achieve 1.000 precision on guardrail and delegation lookups vs 0.013 and 0.077 for unstructured text search.
Exposed_Security_Function: 8-field canonical Agent Flight Recorder, SHA-256 hash chain + 100-event Merkle batching, and Base Sepolia L2 32-byte epoch root anchoring.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Section VI-A (p. 8) enumerates 6 explicit limitations: actions bypassing the instrumented gateway or within-epoch event suppression before anchoring are undetectable from the log alone, and after full host compromise newly written entries cannot be guaranteed true without TEE attestation.
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1) & Section VI-A (p. 8): "The full system adds ~48 us median per-event latency and 512 bytes per event. L2 anchoring costs $2.30 per 100K events at 100-event epochs. The full integrity stack detects edit, delete, reorder, and fork tampering at 100% with zero false positives. Structured forensic queries achieve 1.0 precision on guardrail and delegation lookups where unstructured text search yields 0.013 and 0.077 respectively."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Agent Flight Recorder binds 8 semantic fields per action into SHA-256 hash chains and 100-event Merkle trees anchored on Base Sepolia L2 at ~48 us median per-event latency, 512 B/event, and $2.30 per 100K events, detecting 100% of edit/delete/reorder/fork tampering.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: 5-configuration ablation on synthetic workloads, real SWE-bench traces, and 100 live Base Sepolia L2 anchoring transactions (9 pp.).
Protected_Object: Long-horizon agent audit trails (8 semantic fields: intent, delegation, guardrail, tool execution) and 32-byte on-chain epoch roots.
Composition_Evidence: Links initial user intent and delegation metadata (B1) to tamper-evident SHA-256/Merkle audit logs and L2 blockchain anchors (B4).

Memvalidasi arsitektur Agent Flight Recorder (SHA-256 chain + Merkle tree 100-event epochs + Base Sepolia L2 anchor) beserta seluruh metrik RQ3 (~48 us median latency, 512 B/event, $2.30/100K events, 100% tamper detection, 1.0 vs 0.013/0.077 forensic precision, Table I hlm. 6).

Study_Title: Do User-Authored Permission Policies Improve Protection Against AI Agent Overreach?
Threat_Attacker_Model: AI agent action overreach across email, files, payments, and personal data (7 overreach actions embedded in an 18-action simulated day) when non-expert users author standing consequence-category permission policies (`allow`, `ask`, `never`).
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: NONE (Randomized 3-condition human-subjects experiment comparing per-action Human-in-the-Loop HITL, automated LLM per-action review AUTO, and user-authored standing consequence policies POLICY across N=113 non-programmer participants).
Enforcement_Point_Location: User-facing permission policy authoring and runtime approval interface mapping tool calls into 4 plain-language consequence categories (Sections 3–5, pp. 3–10).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Empirically demonstrates that coarse user-authored standing policies (`POLICY`) reduce overreach protection compared to per-action `HITL` (-20.1 pp) and `AUTO` (-14.5 pp) without reliably reducing total supervision time.
Trust_Assumptions: User study fixes researcher-checked action-to-category mappings so live LLM classification errors do not confound the human policy comparison (explicitly noted p. 2).
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Across N=113 participants supervising an 18-action day (11 required, 7 overreach, Abstract p. 1, Section 4 pp. 6–9): `POLICY` blocked significantly less overreach than `HITL` (-20.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-32.1, -8.1]) and `AUTO` (-14.5 percentage points, 95% CI [-25.8, -3.2]); participants selected `ask` for 114/140 (81.4%) standing rules, reducing runtime prompts from 18.0 to 10.9 but yielding no net time savings once rule-setup time was included, and 133 of 148 executed overreach actions in `POLICY` were approved by humans at runtime.
Exposed_Security_Function: Empirical human-factors benchmark of user-authored consequence policies (`POLICY`) vs. per-action `HITL` and `AUTO` agent supervision.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Simulated 18-action single-day study with online non-technical participants and no real financial/data loss consequences, using 4 coarse fixed consequence categories (Section 6, p. 11).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1): "We analyzed 113 participants without professional software backgrounds across three permission conditions: per-action human-in-the-loop approval (HITL), automated per-action review by a model (AUTO), or user-authored consequence policy (POLICY)... POLICY blocked less overreach than HITL (-20.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-32.1, -8.1]) and AUTO (-14.5 percentage points, 95% CI [-25.8, -3.2]), while required-action completion remained high."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: In a 113-participant study across an 18-action simulated day, user-authored standing consequence policies (POLICY) blocked significantly less agent overreach than per-action HITL (-20.1 pp) and automated review AUTO (-14.5 pp), with 133/148 overreaches approved after runtime escalation.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Controlled 113-participant human-subjects experiment comparing HITL, AUTO, and POLICY across 18 agent actions (15 pp.).
Protected_Object: User email, file, payment, and personal-data tool actions under human/policy supervision.
Composition_Evidence: Reveals how upfront standing policy delegation (B1) interacts negatively with runtime confirmation fatigue (B2), causing higher overreach approval rates.
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (15 hlm.). Memvalidasi studi empiris faktor manusia N=113 pada kebijakan izin pengguna (POLICY memblokir lebih sedikit overreach dibanding HITL sebesar -20.1 pp dan AUTO sebesar -14.5 pp; 114/140 aturan disetel ke 'ask'; 133/148 overreach disetujui manusia saat runtime).
Required_Additional_Evidence: NONE (Teks lengkap PDF ter-pin 15 hlm. telah diaudit dan diekstraksi lengkap 38 kolom oleh REVIEWER_2).

Study_Title: Agentic JWT: A Secure Delegation Protocol for Autonomous AI Agents
Threat_Attacker_Model: OAuth 2.0 bearer-token misuse in autonomous multi-agent systems: stochastic privilege expansion, prompt-injection intent hijacking, cross-agent token replay, and in-process sub-agent impersonation where multiple agents share a single OS process.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Agentic JWT (`A-JWT`): dual-faceted JWS/JWT token carrying a one-way SHA-256 `agent_checksum` hash (derived from the agent's system prompt, tool schemas, and configuration), chained delegation assertions, RFC 7800 Proof-of-Possession (PoP) per-agent keys, and an optional TEE attestation profile.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Lightweight Python A-JWT Client Shim Library (runtime code self-verification, intent token minting, workflow step tracking, PoP key derivation) and API Resource Server Verifier (Sections III–V, pp. 4–13).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Cryptographic binding of each API call to verifiable user intent, workflow step order, and immutable agent configuration checksum (`agent_checksum`), preventing replay, scope violation, and in-process agent impersonation.
Trust_Assumptions: Identity Provider (IdP) and API Resource Server verify `agent_checksum` and PoP signatures; client shim (or optional TEE enclave) protects per-agent derived PoP keys.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Python proof-of-concept evaluation on commodity hardware (Abstract p. 1–2, Section VI p. 14): functional blocking of scope-violating requests, token replay, in-process impersonation, and prompt-injection pathways incurs <1 ms (sub-millisecond) token verification overhead and <2 ms with the checksum client shim / optional TEE attestation profile.
Exposed_Security_Function: Agentic JWT (`A-JWT`), `agent_checksum` OAuth authorization grant, per-agent Proof-of-Possession (PoP) key derivation, and runtime client shim.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Authors note (Abstract p. 1 & Section VII p. 14) that short-lived/one-time intent tokens increase IdP token-minting frequency and that comprehensive large-scale performance/security benchmark tables are deferred to a forthcoming journal submission; uses classical JWT/PoP signatures (STAGE_0).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1–2): "This paper describes Agentic JWT (A-JWT), a dual-faceted token design that binds each agent action to a cryptographically verifiable user intent and optionally to a workflow step. A-JWT carries an agent's identity as a one-way checksum hash derived from its prompt, tools and configuration and a chained delegation assertion... show functional blocking of scope-violating requests, replay, impersonation, and prompt-injection pathways with sub-millisecond overhead on commodity hardware... detect in-process impersonation with < 2 ms overhead."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Agentic JWT (A-JWT) extends OAuth 2.0 with an `agent_checksum` grant (hashing prompt, tools, and config), chained delegation claims, and per-agent Proof-of-Possession keys, blocking replay and in-process impersonation with <2 ms overhead.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Protocol specification, threat model, and Python proof-of-concept functional & microbenchmark evaluation (17 pp.).
Protected_Object: OAuth 2.0 delegation tokens, agent prompt/tool configurations (`agent_checksum`), workflow step transitions, and API endpoints.
Composition_Evidence: Binds user intent and workflow step (B1) to chained sub-agent delegation assertions and `agent_checksum` identity (B2) verified at API tool execution (B3).
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (17 hlm.). Memvalidasi protokol Agentic JWT (A-JWT) dengan grant `agent_checksum`, Proof-of-Possession keys, dan shim runtime (<1 ms verifikasi, <2 ms deteksi impersonasi in-process).
Required_Additional_Evidence: NONE (Teks lengkap PDF ter-pin 17 hlm. telah diaudit dan diekstraksi lengkap 38 kolom oleh REVIEWER_2).

Study_Title: Zero-Knowledge Predicate Proofs Between AI Agents: A Measured, Cross-Protocol Gateway and the Source-Integrity Gap
Threat_Attacker_Model: Over-sharing of raw private data between collaborating agents or prompt-injectable natural-language self-reports of policy compliance across MCP and A2A protocols, compounded by the Source-Integrity Gap (where a prover commits to a fabricated value divorced from the system of record).
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Bulletproofs zero-knowledge range/predicate proofs over Pedersen commitments (C = vG + rH on secp256k1), SHA-256 hash-chained append-only audit logs (`h_i = SHA256(h_{i-1} || entry_i)`), and bi-directional cryptographic fusion with Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) enclave attestation.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Cross-Protocol Zero-Knowledge Proof Gateway exposing a unified proof slot over both Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) on Kubernetes (Sections II–V, pp. 2–7).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Zero-knowledge data minimization (proving governance predicates such as 32-bit order limits without revealing raw values) and bi-directional source-to-proof binding when fused with enclave attestation.
Trust_Assumptions: Discrete-log hardness on secp256k1 (for Pedersen commitments and Bulletproofs) and SHA-256 collision resistance hold; closing the Source-Integrity Gap requires the data-fetching connector to run inside an attested TEE enclave (Section V, pp. 6–7).
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Measured on 1 commodity vCPU and deployed on Kubernetes (Abstract p. 1, Section IV p. 4): a 32-bit threshold predicate proves in 6.2 ms and verifies in 1.0 ms with a 608-byte Bulletproofs proof (64-bit proof is 688 bytes verifying in 3.2 ms; aggregated multi-hop proof takes ~173 ms proving time while cutting proof size from 10,752 B and halving verification time); passes 11/11 adversarial experiments and 19/19 protocol checks.
Exposed_Security_Function: Cross-protocol (MCP + A2A) Bulletproofs Zero-Knowledge Predicate Proof Gateway, SHA-256 hash-chained audit log, and enclave-fused source attestation.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Explicitly highlights the Source-Integrity Gap (p. 1–2): without TEE enclave attestation binding the system of record, a compromised prover agent can generate a valid ZK proof over a lied committed value; secp256k1 Pedersen/Bulletproofs are pre-quantum (STAGE_0_PRE_QUANTUM_ONLY).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1) & Section III–IV (pp. 3–4): "A 32-bit threshold predicate proves in 6.2 ms and verifies in 1.0 ms with a 608-byte Bulletproofs proof on one commodity vCPU; eleven adversarial experiments and nineteen protocol checks pass; and the system is deployed to Kubernetes with empirically verified network isolation... We then address the limitation no comparable work resolves: a predicate proof binds a statement to a committed value, never to the system of record. We give a construction fusing an enclave attestation with the proof in both directions."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Implements a cross-protocol (MCP and A2A) Zero-Knowledge Proof Gateway using secp256k1 Bulletproofs/Pedersen commitments, SHA-256 audit chains, and TEE enclave fusion, proving 32-bit predicates in 6.2 ms and verifying in 1.0 ms (608-byte proof).
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Kubernetes-deployed MCP/A2A ZK gateway evaluated across 11 adversarial experiments, 19 protocol checks, and Bulletproofs latency/size benchmarks (11 pp.).
Protected_Object: Private numerical/categorical enterprise data in cross-agent MCP/A2A predicate checks and SHA-256 audit trails.
Composition_Evidence: Carries Bulletproofs predicate proofs across A2A peer negotiation (B2) and MCP tool calls (B3) while chaining proof hashes in a SHA-256 audit log (B4).
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (11 hlm.). Memvalidasi Zero-Knowledge Proof Gateway lintas MCP & A2A berbasis Bulletproofs/Pedersen secp256k1 (prove 6.2 ms, verify 1.0 ms, 608 B; 11 eksperimen adversarial; 19 cek protokol; fusi enclave untuk Source-Integrity Gap).
Required_Additional_Evidence: NONE (Teks lengkap PDF ter-pin 11 hlm. telah diaudit dan diekstraksi lengkap 38 kolom oleh REVIEWER_2).

Study_Title: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification and Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
Threat_Attacker_Model: Three protocol-level architectural vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification: (1) absence of capability attestation (arbitrary permission claims), (2) bidirectional `sampling/createMessage` without origin authentication (server-side prompt injection), and (3) implicit trust propagation in multi-server compositions.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: NONE (Formal architectural security analysis of MCP violating Least Privilege, Origin Authentication, and Isolation properties, paired with the PROTOAMP benchmark harness).
Enforcement_Point_Location: MCP Host–Server JSON-RPC protocol interface across 5 MCP server implementations evaluated via PROTOAMP (Sections III–IV, pp. 2–5).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Proves that MCP's baseline specification violates Least Privilege, Origin Authentication, and Isolation, amplifying Attack Success Rate (ASR) by 23%–41% over equivalent non-MCP tool integrations.
Trust_Assumptions: Agent host connects to one or more MCP servers following the standard unextended MCP specification.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Evaluated via PROTOAMP across 847 attack scenarios and 5 MCP server implementations (Abstract p. 1, Table VII p. 5): MCP's architectural design amplifies Attack Success Rate (ASR) by 23%–41% compared to equivalent non-MCP direct tool integrations (reaching 52.8%–61.4% baseline MCP ASR).
Exposed_Security_Function: Formal MCP specification vulnerability analysis and PROTOAMP 847-scenario comparative protocol benchmark.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Demonstrates that implementation-level hardening cannot fix MCP's architectural vulnerabilities without protocol-level extensions (such as ATTESTMCP).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1): "We present the first rigorous security analysis of MCP's architectural design, identifying three fundamental protocol-level vulnerabilities: (1) absence of capability attestation allowing servers to claim arbitrary permissions, (2) bidirectional sampling without origin authentication enabling server-side prompt injection, and (3) implicit trust propagation in multi-server configurations... Through controlled experiments on 847 attack scenarios across five MCP server implementations, we demonstrate that MCP's architectural choices amplify attack success rates by 23–41% compared to equivalent non-MCP integrations."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Identifies three protocol-level vulnerabilities in the MCP specification and demonstrates across 847 attack scenarios on 5 MCP server implementations (PROTOAMP) that MCP amplifies attack success rates by 23%–41% over non-MCP integrations.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: Formal protocol property analysis and 847-scenario comparative evaluation across 5 MCP servers (7 pp.).
Protected_Object: MCP server capability declarations, bidirectional `sampling` messages, and multi-server shared context.
Composition_Evidence: Shows how compromising a single low-privilege MCP server at B2 propagates laterally across shared host context to high-privilege MCP servers at B3 (+23%–41% ASR amplification).
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (7 hlm.). Memvalidasi analisis formal 3 kerentanan protokol MCP dan benchmark PROTOAMP (847 skenario serangan pada 5 implementasi server MCP: amplifikasi ASR 23%–41%, Table VII hlm. 5).
Required_Additional_Evidence: NONE (Teks lengkap PDF ter-pin 7 hlm. telah diaudit dan diekstraksi lengkap 38 kolom oleh REVIEWER_2).

Study_Title: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification and Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
Threat_Attacker_Model: Arbitrary capability claiming, unauthenticated server-side `sampling` injection, replay, and cross-server trust propagation in MCP deployments.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: ATTESTMCP backward-compatible protocol extension: CA-signed capability attestation certificates (`x509`/`Ed25519` style server capability manifests) and per-message `HMAC-SHA256` authentication (`mcpsec` header with `server_id`, `timestamp`, 32-byte `nonce`, and `hmac`, Section V, pp. 5–6).
Enforcement_Point_Location: ATTESTMCP Host–Server JSON-RPC middleware verifying capability certificates at session init, enforcing per-server context isolation, and checking `HMAC-SHA256` on every message (Section V, pp. 5–6).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Authenticated server origin, least-privilege capability bounding, and cross-server context isolation, reducing MCP Attack Success Rate from 52.8% to 12.4%.
Trust_Assumptions: Capability Authority (CA) keys and shared `HMAC-SHA256` session keys are uncompromised; legitimately authorized servers can still serve malicious content within their attested scope (explicitly noted in Section VI Limitations, p. 6).
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Across the 847-scenario PROTOAMP benchmark (Abstract p. 1, Table VII p. 5, Table IX p. 6): ATTESTMCP reduces overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 52.8% (and 61.4% with zero isolation) to 12.4% while maintaining 87.6% task completion utility, with a median latency overhead of 8.3 ms per message (`HMAC-SHA256` computation is 0.8 ms, Table IX p. 6).
Exposed_Security_Function: ATTESTMCP capability attestation verifier, `HMAC-SHA256` JSON-RPC message authenticator (`mcpsec`), and cross-server context isolator.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Section VI (p. 6) explicitly lists 4 residual limitations: attacks within a single legitimately-authorized server (12.4% residual ASR), social engineering of users to approve malicious capabilities, CA compromise, and Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU) first-contact attacks.

Study_Title: Attested Tool-Server Admission: A Security Extension to the Model Context Protocol
Threat_Attacker_Model: Unmediated third-party MCP server admission where an agent connects to untrusted external servers (e.g., forged or over-privileged Gmail/Calendar/Drive MCP servers), accepts self-declared tool lists without sensitivity clearance checks, or invokes unapproved high-risk tools.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Offline-signed Ed25519 clearance assertions (`/.well-known/mcp-clearance.json`) over canonical JSON bodies verified against a pinned host trust root (`keyId`, Ed25519 public key, maximum allowed `Clearance` levels, `notAfter` expiry), paired with a deny-by-default per-server tool allowlist and tamper-evident audit log (`mcp-attested`).
Enforcement_Point_Location: MCP Host Admission & Tool-Dispatch Gate (`mcp-attested` in `enclawed-oss` and `enclaved` distributions) verifying `/.well-known/mcp-clearance.json` before server admission and checking the per-server tool allowlist before every tool call (Sections 3–5, pp. 5–11).
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Properties 1–3 (Section 6, p. 10): Authenticated & clearance-bounded server admission (under Ed25519 EUF-CMA), deny-by-default per-server tool least privilege, and complete admission/dispatch auditability with RFC 2119 conformance vectors.
Trust_Assumptions: Host pinned trust root (`keyId` -> Ed25519 public key and max clearance) is intact; Ed25519 is unforgeable (or replaceable by FIPS 186-5 ECDSA P-256/RSA-PSS in FIPS mode, Section 6.3, p. 11).
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Evaluated via machine-checkable conformance vectors and an LLM-driven adversarial coverage campaign (`llama3.2`, 1,500 rounds/phase across forged assertions and disallowed tool calls, Table 1, p. 14): the deterministic Ed25519 admission gate and allowlist gate denied 100% of distinct adversarial inputs with 0 unauthorized network writes (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20349263).
Exposed_Security_Function: Ed25519 `/.well-known/mcp-clearance.json` server admission verifier, deny-by-default per-server tool allowlist, flavor-gated hard-deny enforcement, and RFC 2119 MCP addendum specification.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Section 8 (p. 18) explicitly notes that clearance assertions bind sensitivity levels at the server granularity rather than per-tool, and short-lived per-assertion freshness/revocation (`notBefore`/online CRL) beyond per-signer `notAfter` remains future work; uses classical Ed25519 (STAGE_0).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: [KUTIPAN VERBATIM] Abstract (p. 1) & Section 7 Table 1 (pp. 12–14): "We close it with three additive mechanisms: (1) a small, offline-signed clearance assertion a server publishes at a well-known Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) and a host verifies against a pinned trust root before any tool dispatch; (2) a deny-by-default per-server tool allowlist, so admitting a server is not trusting its every tool; and (3) a flavor-gated enforcement mode that turns the checks from warnings into hard denials, with every decision written to a tamper-evident audit log."
Claim_Text_As_Reported: mcp-attested extends MCP with Ed25519-signed well-known server clearance assertions, pinned trust-root verification, and deny-by-default per-server tool allowlists (Properties 1–3), denying 100% of adversarial inputs across a 1,500-round/phase fuzzing campaign with zero unauthorized network writes.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: RFC 2119 normative specification, open-source implementation (`enclawed-oss`), security property analysis (Properties 1–3), and 1,500-round/phase adversarial evaluation (22 pp.).
Protected_Object: MCP server admission (`/.well-known/mcp-clearance.json`), per-server exposed tool sets, sensitivity clearance levels, and admission audit logs.
Composition_Evidence: Gates external MCP server discovery/admission via Ed25519 clearance assertions (B2), restricts individual tool dispatch via per-server allowlists (B3), and records all admission/dispatch verdicts in a tamper-evident audit log (B4). Same author/platform family as ARXIV-S-0123 (SF-ARXIV-S-0123).
Coding_Rationale: Ekstraksi teks lengkap PDF (22 hlm.). Memvalidasi ekstensi `mcp-attested` (Ed25519 clearance assertion + pinned trust root + deny-by-default tool allowlist + audit log), Properties 1–3 (hlm. 10), dan kampanye pengujian adversarial 1.500 putaran/fase (Table 1 hlm. 14: 100% ditolak, 0 network writes). Satu keluarga platform (Enclawed) dengan ARXIV-S-0123.
